A beret is a type of hat — specifically a soft, round, flat hat with no brim.

Picture a soft, floppy circle of fabric sitting on someone's head. It has no stiff brim sticking out (unlike a baseball cap), no hard structure, and no pointy top (unlike a wizard's hat). It's completely flat and flexible. At the very center of the top, there is usually a tiny, short stem or nub — almost like the stem of an apple, but much smaller.

Because it is soft and has no rigid shape of its own, a beret naturally drapes and slouches. When worn, it tends to hang off to one side of the head, giving it a tilted, slightly lopsided look. That characteristic tilt is actually part of its identity — you almost never see a beret worn perfectly centered and straight like a hard hat.

The rim of a beret fits snugly just above the ears and across the forehead, while the rest of the fabric fans out and hangs over one side.

Berets are usually made from soft, flexible materials — most commonly wool or felt. You can also find them made from cotton or synthetic fabrics. Because of their material, they're comfortable, lightweight, and easy to fold up and carry in a pocket or bag.

They come in virtually any color, but the most classic and widely recognized versions are black, red, navy blue, and olive green.

Berets are worn in two very different worlds: fashion/culture and the military.

In everyday life and culture, the beret is strongly associated with artists, intellectuals, and creative people. If you've ever seen a cartoon or illustration of a painter — someone standing before a canvas with a brush in hand — there's a good chance they're wearing a beret. This image has been around for so long that the beret has become almost a symbol of the artistic and bohemian lifestyle. It is also deeply tied to French culture. When people imagine a stereotypical French person — especially a Parisian — they often picture someone in a beret. This association has made the beret a recognizable symbol of France around the world, even though the hat itself predates modern France and was worn across many European cultures.

In the military, the beret is used as an official part of the uniform in many armies across the world. Here, the color of the beret carries significant meaning — it indicates which unit or branch of the military a soldier belongs to. For example:

  • A green beret is famously associated with the United States Army Special Forces (so much so that these elite soldiers are simply called "the Green Berets").
  • A maroon or red beret is often worn by paratroopers (soldiers who parachute from aircraft).
  • A black beret has been used by various tank and armored units.
  • A blue beret is commonly worn by United Nations peacekeeping forces.

In this military context, the beret is not just a hat — it is a mark of identity, rank, and belonging.

The beret is almost always worn tilted. The rim sits around the head like a headband, and the fabric is pulled or angled to one side — usually the right or left — so that it droops down over that side of the head. The nub at the center gets tucked or pointed in the direction of the drape. This tilted style is the standard way a beret is worn, and it's part of what makes it visually distinctive from other hats.

• She pulled on her black beret, tilting it to one side before heading out into the rainy Paris morning.
  • The soldier's green beret told everyone he was part of an elite special forces unit.
  • The old painter sat in the café, beret on his head, sketchbook open on the table.

In short, a beret is a soft, round, flat, brimless hat — worn tilted to one side — that stands at the intersection of art, culture, fashion, and military tradition. It is one of the most recognizable hat shapes in the world, partly because of its simple and distinctive silhouette, and partly because of the strong cultural images it calls to mind: the French artist, the bohemian intellectual, and the elite soldier.
